Bromsgrove.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of north Worcestershire
s1loc: Bromsgrove anchors a north Worcestershire visitor economy built around Avoncroft Museum of Historic Buildings, England's first open-air museum, where more than twenty-five rescued structures and the National Telephone Kiosk Collection spread across nineteen acres at Stoke Heath. The Elizabethan Grafton Manor and the Palladian Hagley Hall, set in its 350-acre deer park, give the old nail-making town genuine heritage pull for visitors arriving off the M5 and M42.

The leisure and activity layer runs into the Clent Hills and the 524-acre Lickey Hills Country Park, where Beacon Hill rises near 1,000 feet for far-reaching views over Worcestershire. Sanders Park sits in the heart of town with its gardens and play areas, and the Tardebigge flight on the Worcester and Birmingham Canal, the longest lock flight in the country, draws walkers, cyclists and narrowboaters through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Artrix arts venue, with its live music, theatre and film programme, and the medieval St John the Baptist Church, whose churchyard holds the celebrated Bromsgrove Guild graves. The town's Bromsgrove Court Leet, the poet A E Housman links and the long-running Bromsgrove Festival keep an events calendar turning across the market centre and the surrounding villages of Tardebigge and Stoke Prior.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base, country-house stays at Grafton Manor and a guide scene built around the museum and the hills. Bromsgrove railway station on the Cross City Line links Birmingham and Worcester, the M5 and M42 corridor puts the wider region within an easy day trip, and the draw of the Lickeys and the Severn valley feeds a steady seasonal flow into the area.

Stratford-upon-Avon.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of Shakespeare's Stratford
s1loc: Stratford-upon-Avon runs one of the country's best-known visitor economies, built on the five Shakespeare houses cared for by the Shakespeare Birthplace Trust. Shakespeare's Birthplace on Henley Street, Anne Hathaway's Cottage at Shottery, Hall's Croft, Mary Arden's Farm at Wilmcote and the New Place garden draw international crowds, while Holy Trinity Church on the Avon, where Shakespeare was baptised and buried, anchors the historic riverside.

The leisure and activity layer keeps families busy across the Stratford Butterfly Farm, the MAD Museum and Tudor World on Sheep Street, with rowing boats, river cruises and paddleboarding on the River Avon. Bancroft Gardens and the Recreation Ground line the waterfront beside the canal basin, and the Stratford Distillery and Avon Boating trips give visitors and day-trippers plenty to fill the warmer season.

Heritage and culture run deepest at the Royal Shakespeare Company, whose Royal Shakespeare Theatre and Swan Theatre sit on the riverbank alongside The Other Place studio. The Shakespeare birthday celebrations each April fill the town with a costumed procession, flag ceremonies and live music in Bancroft Gardens, anchoring an events calendar that runs through the Gower Memorial, the Guild Chapel and the old timber-framed quarter.

The visitor trade leans on a deep hotel base of more than fifty properties, from The Arden Hotel opposite the theatres to riverside and Tudor inns, with a busy tour-operator and guide scene. Stratford-upon-Avon railway station links Birmingham and London Marylebone, the coaches roll in off the M40, and the draw of Warwick Castle and the Cotswolds feeds a year-round and seasonal flow of visitors into south Warwickshire.

Spalding.region: Spalding and the South Holland fens
Spalding.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of South Holland
s1loc: Spalding sits on the River Welland at the heart of the South Holland fens, and its marquee draw is Springfields, the designer outlet whose Festival Gardens blaze with daffodils and tulips each spring in tribute to the town's bulb-growing past. The grade I listed Ayscoughfee Hall, over 550 years old, holds the town museum and five acres of gardens with a Lutyens-designed war memorial, anchoring a Georgian centre lined with merchants' houses.

The leisure and activity layer runs from the Springfields Adventure Land family attraction to the Spalding Water Taxi, which cruises the River Welland between the town centre and the gardens. The Pinchbeck Marsh and the wider fen drains give anglers, walkers and cyclists flat waterside routes, and the Baytree owl demonstrations and garden attraction at Weston keep families and day visitors busy across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Spalding Gentlemen's Society on Broad Street, founded in 1710 and the oldest provincial learned society in the country, with its remarkable museum collection. The South Holland Centre arts venue, theatre and cinema runs a year-round programme, and the famous Spalding Flower Parade, with its bulb-decorated floats, fills the streets each spring as the headline event in the fenland calendar.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base and a guide scene built around the gardens and the river. Spalding railway station links Peterborough, Lincoln and the East Coast Main Line at Grantham, the A16 and A17 carry day-trippers across the fens, and the draw of the bulb fields, Boston's Stump and the Lincolnshire coast feeds a steady seasonal flow of visitors into South Holland.

Newark.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of the Trent valley
s1loc: Newark-on-Trent runs a busy Nottinghamshire visitor economy around Newark Castle, which has stood nearly 900 years on the banks of the River Trent and where King John died in 1216. The National Civil War Centre in the Old Magnus Buildings tells the gripping story of the town's three sieges, and the towering St Mary Magdalene Church, one of the largest parish churches in England, dominates the historic Market Square.

The leisure and activity layer runs into Sconce and Devon Park, built around the 17th-century Queen's Sconce earthwork with its woodland paths, play areas and cafe, and out to the Newark Air Museum at Winthorpe, whose collection of more than ninety aircraft and cockpits fills two display halls. The Trent and the Riverside Park, the marina and the towpaths give walkers, cyclists and boaters waterside routes through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Palace Theatre, which has entertained the town for over a century with music, comedy and drama just off the Market Square, and the National Civil War Trail that threads augmented-reality stops from the castle to the Queen's Sconce. The Newark International Antiques and Collectors Fair, the largest of its kind in Europe, and the riverside Newark Festival each summer headline an events calendar at the Newark Showground.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base, including The Grange Hotel and riverside inns, and a guide scene built around the castle and the air museum. Newark Northgate on the East Coast Main Line reaches London in under ninety minutes, Newark Castle station connects Lincoln and Nottingham, and the A1 and the draw of Lincoln and Sherwood feed a steady seasonal flow of visitors into the Trent valley.

Brentwood.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of west Essex
s1loc: Brentwood anchors a west Essex visitor economy with Brentwood Cathedral, a striking neo-classical landmark redesigned in the 1990s around its Victorian Gothic church, at the centre of the town. The Elizabethan Ingatestone Hall, the long-time seat of the Petre family, opens its panelled rooms, priest holes and grounds to visitors just outside town, while the high street, the Sir Antony Browne associations and the old coaching-route heritage give the market centre real depth.

The leisure and activity layer spreads across Thorndon Country Park, 500 acres of ancient woodland, ponds and giant oak pollards home to the Gruffalo Trail, and the 520-acre Weald Country Park with its deer herd and Stick Man trail. Old MacDonald's Farm on the outskirts brings tractor rides and animal feeding for younger visitors, while Hartswood and South Weald keep walkers, cyclists and families busy through the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Brentwood Theatre, a community venue serving more than forty performing-arts groups beside The Hermitage in the town centre, and the Warley Place nature reserve, the lost garden of plantswoman Ellen Willmott. Old St Peter's Chapel, the Brentwood Museum in Warley and a calendar of high-street and country-park events keep a cultural and seasonal programme turning across the borough.

The visitor trade leans on a town and roadside hotel base, including the Marygreen Manor and roadside chains, and a guide scene built around the country parks and the cathedral. Brentwood and Shenfield stations put the Elizabeth line and Liverpool Street within reach, the A12 and M25 carry day-trippers in from London and the wider county, and the draw of Epping Forest feeds a steady seasonal flow into west Essex.

Redhill.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of east Surrey
s1loc: Redhill anchors an east Surrey visitor economy at the foot of the North Downs, with the Harlequin Theatre and Cinema the cultural heart of the town and a year-round programme of theatre, comedy, film and pantomime. Nearby Reigate adds Reigate Priory and its 200-acre park, the medieval Reigate Castle grounds and the famous Reigate Caves, giving the pairing of towns a genuine heritage and visitor pull off the M25.

The leisure and activity layer runs into Gatton Park, a Capability Brown landscape of gardens, lakes and trails on the National Trust's Reigate Hill and Gatton estate, where the 19th-century Reigate Fort tops a chalk escarpment with sweeping views. Earlswood Lakes and its nature reserve, the Redhill Aerodrome and the Surrey Hills bridleways give walkers, anglers, cyclists and flyers plenty across the warmer season.

Heritage and culture centre on the Belfry Shopping Centre and pedestrianised High Street, the Royal Earlswood with its Victorian past, and the heathland of Reigate Heath with its windmill church, the only consecrated working windmill in England. The villages of Merstham, Nutfield and Bletchingley, the North Downs Way and a calendar of seasonal fairs and walks at Gatton Park keep a cultural programme turning across the borough.

The visitor trade leans on a town hotel base and the Victorian-mansion stays at Nutfield Priory just east of town, with a guide scene built around the Downs and the parks. Redhill station sits at the junction of the Brighton Main Line and North Downs Line, with direct trains to London Victoria, London Bridge and Gatwick Airport just seven miles south, feeding a steady commuter and seasonal flow into east Surrey.

Bramhall.s1_head: Kitting the visitor economy of south Stockport
s1loc: Bramhall anchors a south Stockport visitor economy around Bramall Hall, a superb black-and-white timber-framed Tudor manor whose oldest parts date from the 14th century, set in seventy acres of Victorian Romantic parkland. Its sixteen rooms hold celebrated 16th-century wall paintings, an Elizabethan plaster ceiling and the Victorian kitchens and servants' quarters, and the rooftop Scale the Scaffold tours take visitors high onto the grade I listed roof above the brooks and lakes.

The leisure and activity layer runs across Bramall Park, with its woodland walks, formal gardens, three man-made ponds and the Stables Kitchen cafe open seven days a week, and out to the Happy Valley and Ladybrook Valley Interest Trail along the brook. The Carrs Wood, the Lady Brook and the Bramhall recreation grounds give families, walkers and cyclists green routes through the warmer season, with the May duck race drawing thousands to the park.

Heritage and culture centre on the Bramhall village conservation area, the old St Michael and All Angels Church and the timber-framed character of the suburb, with the hall's events and weddings calendar at its core. Neighbouring Stockport adds the Air Raid Shelters, the Hat Works museum and the Stockport Plaza, while Bramhall's own seasonal fairs and the parkland concerts keep a cultural programme turning across the year.

The visitor trade leans on a suburban hotel and inn base, with a guide scene built around the hall and the country parks, and easy reach of the wider Cheshire draw. Bramhall railway station links Stockport and Manchester Piccadilly, the A6 and M60 put the city and the Peak District within an easy day trip, and the pull of Wilmslow, Lyme Park and the Cheshire countryside feeds a steady seasonal flow into south Stockport.
